items.passage: Walk through the oldest quarter of almost any town and the streets refuse to run straight. They bend, narrow without warning, and meet at angles that no planner would choose today. The newer districts nearby are laid out in clean squares, so the contrast is easy to observe. The reason is that those crooked lines were never drawn at all. They were worn. Before anyone owned a map, a track formed where feet and carts found the easiest ground, around a marsh, along the edge of a field, or down to a stream whose location is now hidden under stone. Later, houses were built facing the track, and the track became a street. Because a wall is expensive to move, each new building locked that curve in place, and the shape survived long after the marsh was drained and the field abandoned.
choices: difficulties of moving walls in old quarters
methods of draining marshes for early building
reasons why modern planners prefer clean squares
street shape as a record of unplanned growth
the role of maps in the founding of towns

items.passage: For a long time, painters ground their own colours and mixed them with oil indoors. A stone slab, a jar of oil, and heavy powders were not things an artist could carry, so most pictures of fields and skies were finished from memory or from a few quick sketches. Drawing outdoors was ordinary; completing a serious work there seemed abnormal. Then someone thought to seal freshly mixed paint inside a soft metal tube. That small container changed the working day. A painter could now locate a spot beside a river, open a folding stool, and finish a picture where the light actually fell. Because weather would not wait, brushwork grew faster and looser, and the surface kept the marks of that speed. The first reaction was harsh, and critics called the loose finish a flaw. Later the same looseness was praised as honesty, and studio landscapes looked stiff beside these lively outdoor scenes.
choices: How Critics Learned to Praise Loose Brushwork
A Small Tube That Moved Painting Outdoors
Why Studio Landscapes Were Painted from Memory
Grinding Colours: The Lost Craft of the Painter
Weather, Light, and the Patience of the Artist

items.src: When a river runs low, a reactor goes quiet
items.passage: Romania operates a single nuclear power station, and the building stands on the bank of the Danube. The station draws all of the cooling water for its reactors from that one river. In August a long stretch of hot, dry weather pushed the river far below its usual level. The operator had already idled one of the plant's two reactors during the previous month. On Thursday it powered down the second reactor as well, leaving the station silent. The station normally supplies about a fifth of all the electricity used in Romania. Its director said that no restart was expected within the following ten days. A shutdown of that length forces an immediate rearrangement of the national supply. The government therefore turned to wind generation and to imported power in order to cover the gap. The same shrinking river now presses on neighboring Hungary, whose reactors also draw their cooling water directly from the Danube.
choices: 루마니아의 원자력 발전소는 한 곳이다.
두 원자로는 같은 날 함께 가동을 멈췄다.
발전소는 다뉴브강에서 냉각수를 얻는다.
이 발전소는 루마니아 전력의 약 5분의 1을 공급한다.
정부는 부족분을 풍력과 수입 전력으로 메웠다.
